articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Kali Hays Technology reporter 
- Published 23 November 2026 
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America. 
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US. 
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang. 
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China. 
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed. 
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang. 
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US. 
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology. 
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee. 
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal". 
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years. 
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China. 
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022. 
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China. 
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers. 
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist. 
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry. 
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools. 
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House. 
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%. 
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too. 
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take . 
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal. 
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations. 
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: India pledges $1.6bn to Nepal in reset of ties
articles.summary: As Nepal rebuilds after deadly floods, its prime minister sets contentious issues aside to secure Indian funding, port access and a new train service.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The two prime ministers exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia Correspondent ,  Reporting from Delhi 
- Published 23 November 2026 
Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah has repeatedly called for his country to be treated as an equal by its powerful neighbours. His first visit to the Indian capital, Delhi, put that approach to the test, as both sides sought to reset a relationship strained by years of friction. 
The contrast between the two leaders was striking. 
Shah, 36, wearing his trademark black suit and sunglasses, stood beside Prime Minister Narendra Modi, 76, dressed in white. Shah rose to power after a wave of Gen Z-led protests toppled his predecessor. 
Modi, meanwhile, is serving a third term and has recently faced student-led protests in India. 
Yet, the two leaders seemed determined to project warmer relations. They exchanged gifts, inspected a military guard of honour and jointly flagged off a new cross-border train service. 
For Nepal, the stakes were about far more than repairing diplomatic ties. 
The two countries announced a series of agreements covering trade, hydropower, transport and education for Nepali youths. 
India, more crucially, unveiled a $1.6bn (£1.22bn) support package as Nepal recovers from devastating floods earlier this year. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
According to Nepal's estimates, the cost of rebuilding the region hit by a devastating flash flood in September could amount to $4.8bn 
The floods killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing. Shah's government has faced criticism over support for families which lost homes and loved ones. 
The country faces a huge reconstruction challenge. The government estimates rebuilding could cost as much as $4.8bn. Addressing the UN General Assembly in September, Shah warned that when climate disasters devastate poorer countries, "the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan". 
Modi pledged nearly $1.6bn in Indian support. Most of it will come as a line of credit for energy projects, alongside about $400m in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure. 
While Nepal would have preferred a larger package, former senior Nepali diplomat Vijay Kant Karna says it is still "a significant amount" and could help stabilise a relationship that has often been uneasy. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Although the joint statement acknowledged outstanding issues, the two leaders did not mention the border dispute in their public remarks 
A Hindu-majority nation wedged between India and China, Nepal has long had to navigate competing interests from its two giant neighbours. Allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have frequently complicated ties with India. 
Nepal's former Prime Minister, KP Sharma Oli, who leads a communist party, was widely viewed as being closer to China. Shah, by contrast, emerged as a political outsider when he was elected earlier this year. The former rapper, then 35, led a party that was only four years old. 
His new approach of dealing with India may explain why the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, although the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained. 
According to Govind Pokharel, a former vice-chairman of Nepal's National Planning Commission, Shah's government may have chosen to set contentious issues aside in order to secure progress on more immediate development needs. 
"Right now you can go home and convince the young Nepalis that it will be handled later," Pokhrel says, "but if they don't deal with these issues in the future, there will be criticism." 
Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat says both sides appear to have opted to leave the dispute to established mechanisms rather than engage in what he calls "cartographic aggressions". 
There were other gains for Nepal as a result of the Delhi visit. 
As a landlocked country heavily dependent on India for trade, Nepal secured access to two additional Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip. The two sides also agreed to improve road and rail connectivity. 
The leaders jointly inaugurated a train service linking Ayodhya in India, revered by Hindus as the birthplace of Lord Ram, with Janakpur in Nepal, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of his wife Sita. 
There was, however, disappointment on aviation. 
Nepal has long sought greater access to Indian airspace in order to attract international traffic to its airports at Bhairahawa and Pokhara. 
Some analysts believe the lack of an agreement reflects Indian concerns over Chinese involvement in the two airport projects. 
"The airport in Pokhara can pose certain security challenges for India, so it is a more complicated issue to resolve," says Trigunayat. 
India did, however, agree to make an existing air route linking Kathmandu, Bhairahawa and Lucknow bidirectional. 
"Nepal invested a huge amount of money in those airports," says Pokharel. "It fell short of expectations, but the bidirectional route is a breakthrough." 
Shah must now manage relations with China as he seeks to balance the interests of Nepal's two much larger neighbours. 
For now he returns home with substantial financial commitments from India as Nepal continues the long task of rebuilding.

articles.title: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit
articles.summary: Trade, connectivity and regional cooperation will be on top of the agenda when Nepal's PM meets his India counterpart.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit By Anbarasan Ethirajan Global Affairs Correspondent 
- Published 20 November 2026 
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour. 
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government. 
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials. 
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August. 
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for. 
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles). 
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Nepal suffered devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands missing 
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi. 
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset. 
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC. 
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds. 
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance. 
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre). 
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements. 
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal. 
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests. 
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily. 
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
India and Nepal share an open border and longstanding economic ties 
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further. 
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae. 
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year. 
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences. 
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region. 
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas. 
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC. 
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination. 
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable. 
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance . 
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours. 
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus. 
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations. 
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough. 
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit. 
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office. 
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom. 
While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

articles.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia By Bernd Debusmann Jr ,  White House reporter   and   Kali Hays ,  Technology reporter ,  Reporting from San Francisco 
- Published 23 November 2026 Updated 1 hour ago 
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy. 
The company came under pressure by Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring him back. 
But now both Trump and Nvidia are facing bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, just as Huang is due to testify before Congress next week. 
The CEO's comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that left the S&P 500 in correction territory, and added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value. 
Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value. 
But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price. 
As Asian stock markets opened, Nvidia racked up more gains and helped lift other share prices across the tech sector. 
- 
Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Nvidia's stock skyrockets after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO 
Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." 
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. 
It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him. 
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. 
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO. 
Figure caption, 
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO 
In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO. 
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot." 
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added. 
The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene. 
"Probably so," Trump said. 
- 
The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang 
- Published 13 hours ago 
- 
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? 
- Published 13 hours ago 
Congress vows to investigate Nvidia and the Trump administration's role 
The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang. 
Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years". 
"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says. 
Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls. 
Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed that Congress will conduct "a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation". 
"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said, echoing many lawmakers on Monday who said that Congress must pass strong export control legislation. 
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee. 
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee once Democrats take control of the chamber in January, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless". 
"The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement," she also said. 
Republicans, too, called for answers. 
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," said Republican Representative Don Bacon, who chairs a House subcommittee on cyber security. 
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible." 
The chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back." 
-

- Published 8 hours ago 
-

- Published 12 hours ago 
- 
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal 
- Published 6 hours ago 
Trump's personal Nvidia investments 
Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September. 
A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts. 
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit. 
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures. 
The BBC has contacted the White House. 
Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts. 
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space By Helen Davidson 
- Published 3 hours ago 
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. 
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports. 
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element." 
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously". 
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign". 
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options. 
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said. 
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites. 
Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue". 
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said. 
A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers". 
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported. 
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation. 
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation . 
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time. 
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: What failure of COP31 reveals about a divided world
articles.summary: Interests of oil-producing countries, a US boycott and a dispute over finance may have torpedoed climate talks.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Some have hailed the lack of consensus as a sign of a positive shift, despite the Turkey summit failure By Justin Rowlatt 
Climate Editor 
- Published 23 November 2026 
Some may have found it ironic that the world's biggest conference on climate change should collapse over the very mention of fossil fuels - the main cause of global warming. 
Yet that is what happened in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. 
The failure tells us something about the state of climate diplomacy. But it may tell us even more about the increasingly divided world in which the negotiations take place. 
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who led the negotiations, spoke of a backdrop constituting "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". The competing demands, he said, had become "unbridgeable red lines". 
Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister and the summit's president, was blunter. Governments should not disappoint people desperate for climate action, he suggested, by getting "hung up on one word or phrase". 
And Kurum had a point. Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, there was agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The proposed Antalya Pact failed to mention them at all. 
Was it really worth sacrificing the agreement over two words, then? 
The countries that rejected it said the distinction was fundamental. They argued that there was a world of difference between promising to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and committing to move away from the fuels responsible for most of them. Without that explicit commitment, they feared the new agreement would weaken the one made in Dubai. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Co-leader of the negotiations Chris Bowen blamed the failure to reach an agreement on "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory" 
Normally, it is difficult to establish exactly who has said what at these conferences. Much of the bargaining takes place behind closed doors, and governments are often reluctant to admit which proposals they have opposed. 
This time, some of the opposition was public - mostly from oil-producing nations. 
Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking on behalf of the 22 Arab League countries, argued that Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions. It was wealthy industrialised nations, he said, that bore the overwhelming responsibility for the problem. 
He defended the Arab countries' right to choose how to tackle climate change according to their national circumstances. 
Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko went further. Cutting oil and gas supplies before demand fell, he warned, would cause shortages, higher prices and energy poverty. 
"For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel," he said. 
The wider political backdrop was still more revealing. 
The US, which in previous rounds of talks had helped broker compromises - sometimes working alongside China - had no official delegation in Antalya. President Donald Trump has rejected the entire international climate process. 
And while delegates argued over fossil fuels in Turkey, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen that included a pledge to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. 
The priorities of some of the world's most powerful governments appeared very different from those being discussed in the negotiating rooms. 
A majority that may yet offer hope 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, said a deal that did not mention fossil fuels was "unconscionable" 
Yet, perhaps, the picture is more optimistic than it first appears. About 130 governments backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels - roughly two-thirds of the countries represented in Antalya. 
Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker political commitment that might undermine the progress already made. 
Looked at this way, the collapse is not evidence that the world has lost its appetite for climate action. Quite the opposite - a substantial majority of governments were demanding more ambitious action. 
So why not simply find a way for them to move ahead without waiting for the countries determined to block them? 
The difficulty becomes clearer when you look beyond the dispute over fossil fuels. 
Kononuchenko had another target in his sights: climate finance. Much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations, he complained, comes as loans rather than grants. He said that developing countries ended up repaying more than they received. 
"This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner," he declared. 
Then, in a striking moment, he leaned towards the microphone and switched from Russian into English to address his criticism directly to the Europeans: "First of all distinguished representatives of the EU." 
Russia has its own reasons for attacking Europe, but the complaint about finance is one that many developing countries share. They argue that they are being asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving too little help to adapt to climate change or build cleaner economies. 
The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the negotiations began. Mohamed Adow, the Kenyan campaigner who heads Power Shift Africa, accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the failure on finance. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the COP process 
So is it possible for a majority of countries to outvote those blocking progress? 
The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, has acknowledged the need to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible. Others want countries prepared to move faster to make their own agreements outside the formal talks. 
But there is a reason the UN climate process depends on consensus. International climate co-operation is largely voluntary. 
Voting might produce more ambitious agreements on paper, but would it persuade the governments that had been outvoted to act? Consensus also offers some protection to smaller and poorer nations that might otherwise find themselves overruled by the most powerful countries. 
Meanwhile, the failure to agree a summit declaration does not mean climate action stops. Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles are becoming increasingly competitive, while the upheaval in global oil and gas supplies is giving countries another reason to generate their own electricity rather than depend on imported fossil fuels. 
The energy transition is moving forward, whatever happens in the UN negotiating rooms. The problem is that it is not moving nearly fast enough for the climate. 
Figure caption, 
What’s next after no deal at COP31 climate talks? 
- 
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed 
- Published 1 day ago 
- 
Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31 
- Published 23 hours ago 
A rare moment of agreement 
Perhaps the most poignant aspect of the failed Antalya Pact is what the countries had apparently been prepared to accept. 
The final draft expressed "deep concern" that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years. It warned that further warming would cause increasingly serious damage, some of it irreversible, and called for urgent action to limit how far temperatures rose above that threshold. 
This remarkably strong language had survived into the final version, apparently without provoking the opposition that sank the agreement. Even countries bitterly divided over fossil fuels and finance seemed prepared to acknowledge the scale of the danger. 
Yet they couldn't agree on how to respond. 
And that, perhaps, is what Antalya tells us about the state of international climate co-operation. The problem isn't simply finding the right words or changing the voting rules. It is persuading countries with very different interests to take action that no international authority can compel them to take. 
That was always going to be difficult. In today's divided world, it looks harder than ever.

Watch: Carney and Trump impersonators take stage with real Mark Carney By Nadine Yousif Senior Canada reporter 
- Published 23 November 2026 
Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks. 
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech. 
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney. 
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage. 
Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress. 
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala. 
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy." 
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians. 
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra. 
Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator." 
Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration. 
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster , external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's , external support for Trump. 
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media. , external 
Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery. 
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel. 
"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

articles.title: 'I want to destroy capitalism, not France': On the streets with the French ultra left
articles.summary: The BBC meets the far-left protesters French President Emmanuel Macron says are trying to bring down the Republic.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: The BBC's Katya Adler speaks to protesters taking part in recent demonstrations By Katya Adler Europe Editor 
- Published 23 November 2026 
France is in turmoil. Crippling public debt, a "lame-duck" president with six months left in office, and massive social unrest - sparked by student protests which have erupted into looting and violence. 
This Saturday marked the sixth weekend in a row of demos against soaring prices, worsening public services and alleged police brutality. Violence by protesters is down on last month but still present. 
President Emmanuel Macron has publicly blamed riots on "delinquents" and "ultra-left groups" whose aim, he says, is to bring down the French Republic. 
That's quite a claim – and one that needs examining. 
The unrest in France has become a political football ahead of key presidential and parliamentary elections next year. The left in France blames the centre and right for the cost-of-living crisis that's making French people so upset and angry. They blame the hard left for fomenting violence (which they deny). While the nationalist right pledges, if elected, it will return order and security to France's streets. 
So, who exactly are these "ultra-left" groups Macron speaks of? And how organised and dangerous are they? 
It's infamously hard to speak to members of the radical left. They don't much like what they call mainstream media. We're viewed as part of an establishment many of them despise. 
My best bet was to head out into the protests and try to approach people dressed in all black and ski masks or balaclavas (worn, they say, to hide their identity from police). It's a quasi-uniform associated with left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block. 
You see them at demos all over Europe. In France, they tend to appear from city side streets, as daytime protests are dying down, dusk is falling and riot police begin to emerge in full force. 
Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC Image caption, 
The BBC's Katya Adler talking to a protester 
French intelligence drastically underestimated the outpouring of anger, looting and destruction following protests last month. More than 1,000 police officers were reportedly injured, young protesters had bones broken and two reportedly lost a hand in altercations with police armed with stun grenades. Le Monde newspaper has an article , external it is constantly updating to investigate a rising number of reports of protester injuries. The French Insurers Federation estimates damages to shops and private property on 17 October alone - the day of the biggest riots - came to around €207m (£175.5m). 
Since then, the French authorities are trying to tightly manage demos. Police presence is heavy. Protesters say heavy handed. 
Towards the end of one of the protests this month, we saw would-be rioters vastly outnumbered, glass bottles and homemade paint bombs at the ready to throw at police. They were no match for the batons, stun grenades and tear gas the officers had to hand. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
French police pepper spraying protesters during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris earlier this month 
As we were being forcefully kettled in by police, I tried to talk to would-be rioters. Few wanted to engage but I then met 18-year-old Nas (not his real name) and friends. They would only speak to me if they could hide their identity. This was to avoid police detection, they said. 
Milling, you could say provocatively, by baton-at-the-ready police – they seemed to fit a radical-left rioter stereotype. 
"How can you justify the violence?" I ask them. 
"Without violence, you don't achieve anything," one of them tells me. "It's the only way to get our voices heard." 
"We come from an area with a bad reputation. Our schools are a mess. Our teachers quit. You need qualifications to get a decent job. There is supposed to be equality in France. We won't give up our fight." 
These young men, we discover, come from the sprawling housing estates common on French city outskirts - the banlieues - associated with deprivation, unrest and second or third generation immigrant families. 
They weren't politicised or organised by the radical left, they insisted. Just angry. 
Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, 
Left-wing rioters or disruptors, known as the Black Block, tend to dress in all black, wearing ski masks or balaclavas 
Earlier, I had spotted two hard-left student activists, standing masked on top of a bus shelter, above the thronging crowd of protesters waving banners sporting the red anarchist sign and the symbol for the Antifa (anti-fascist) movement. 
I put it to them that France has a proud tradition and respect for the right to protest but that the country has been horrified by the violence it's seen over the last weeks. 
They were keen to downplay the rioting but - again – would only speak if they could remain anonymous. 
"Violence ends up reflecting badly on our movements. We don't like it. But what's a smashed shop window compared to police using stun guns on protesting school kids? Also, people [in France] are regularly going cold and hungry. They're losing faith in this society." 
How could they believe violence would bring about a juster society, I wondered? 
They shrug off my question. In France, these days, the real violence is state violence, they say. 
Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC Image caption, 
Some protesters don't support the Black Block's violence but say the state's violence is worse 
French intelligence estimates there are 5,000 "ultra-left" activists in the country. 
Anticapitalist Starflix (that's his codename) counts himself as one of them. The 17-year-old is also a member of the violent Black Block movement. We'd arranged to meet on the edge of the protest, by a narrow canal. 
Fearful about being apprehended by police, he asked to remain anonymous. 
He showed me a couple of homemade paint-bombs - eggshells filled with paint and sealed with medical tape that he throws at police officers. He carries them in his rucksack, wrapped in a royal blue Italia football shirt. 
"We throw the paint bombs at the visors on riot police helmets, so they have to lift them up in order to see and that makes them suffer their own tear gas that they've sprayed at us," he tells me. 
"We pick up stones and rocks too. Anything we find on the streets of Paris, to throw." 
I put it to him that he and others in the Black Block are causing a lot of problems on French streets: damaging businesses, hurting police officers, destroying the demos for peaceful protesters. What is he trying to achieve? 
As he's under 18, his parents give us permission to speak to him. They share his politics, Starflix tells me, but not all rioters - masked and dressed in black as he is - do. 
"The Black Block isn't a single organisation. It's a technique. Some of us use violence to get government reform. I want to bring about a revolution. 
"Other people are opportunists who use anonymity to steal things. When we all wear the same clothes, it makes it harder for police to identify us." 
When I ask if he is scared he might get hurt or arrested, he admits he is but says what frightens him more is the thought that society might not change. 
Social media plays a huge role in the riots. Starflix tells me he and his friends use Signal and Telegram to arrange to meet at protests. 
Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC Image caption, 
"The Black Block isn't a single organisation," says protester Starflix 
There are numerous websites and Instagram profiles, mainly hosted by left-wing organisations, offering tips for protesters and rioters, such as: keep your phone at home so police can't track you, cover your face to avoid being identified and emulate martial arts expert Bruce Lee and "be like water" - appearing and disappearing into crowds. That's advice passed on by the Hong Kong protesters eight years ago. 
While not formally organising the protests or violence with these posts, could the fact groups host this information online be viewed as a kind of incitement or manipulation of youngsters whose feelings are running so high in France? 
All the young rioters I spoke to insist they are not being herded or directed, but is there something bigger behind what's happening? 
Image source, Lee Durant/BBC Image caption, 
Ultra-left protesters spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity 
It takes our team a long time, but they manage to find a seasoned activist with the Black Block who would speak to us. I put to him Macron's assertion that the ultra left has organised groups that aim to bring down the French Republic. Is that true? 
"It's totally false of the authorities to say we are all organised. And the intelligence services know it," the activist scoffs. "It's a manipulation of the French public to make them think there is an enemy within." 
"Basically, people turn up to a protest, get dressed in black and do their own thing. The uniting factor is rage and not just in France. You see the same rage [in protests] in Italy, Germany, Spain. It's exploding by itself." 
I ask if the anti-capitalist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party (LFI) are somehow linked to the violence. They are present at most protests, supporters handing out campaign pamphlets to the chanting crowds. 
But the activist denies this, telling me Mélenchon is "a capitalist because he's part of the system". He says the LFI and the trade unions try to "calm" unrest, while he believes things need to be "stepped up a notch". 
Why had he decided to talk to us, I ask - does he want to collapse the French government? 
"I just want to say we don't love violence. I don't want to destroy France. We want to destroy a system that is a capitalist system, of course, but to change the society in a way that we think will be better for the most people, for more people. 
"More and more find it hard to make ends meet. In the countryside, people can't even afford to fill their tank with petrol." 
You have to leave the city, heading out into the gloriously autumnal French countryside, to meet some of the more organised, hardcore elements of the ultra left. 
Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC Image caption, 
Limoges Town Hall, allegedly damaged by protesters, has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in 
This is a world of eco activism and known saboteurs. One man remains in police custody linked to the fire during protests at Limoges Town Hall last month . The devastated, yet somehow still elegant, 19th century building has become a symbol of the current state France appears to be in. An acrid smell still hangs in the air one month on. 
The 34-year-old arson suspect, who insists he's innocent, comes from a hamlet near Limoges, known for its anarchist, environmentalist community. His father, a fellow activist, is also known to French intelligence. We approached the father and the suspect's lawyer for comment. They didn't want to speak. 
Instead, we met a 39-year-old father of one, a local full-time ultra-left activist for more than two decades. Like the other individuals we spoke to for this investigation, he would only talk to us on condition he could remain anonymous. 
"We were all shocked by the [town hall] fire – even as we watched it happen in front of us - but it's our duty to take action," he tells me. 
"I can't leave this world to my son in the state that it's in. Look how military vehicles and brute force are used by the state against our young students. 
"It's amazing the people haven't taken up arms against them. Do we need a policeman killed in order for the state to listen?" 
How can you say that, I want to know? 
"As a child, I was educated with French values – liberty, equality, fraternity - but when I look at the social injustice in the world now, I'm disgusted. As a father, I can't let this go on. If I have to, I would take a bullet to protect the youth of this country." 
These are dangerous-sounding words - but the radical left doesn't appear to be big, armed or united enough to seriously threaten France. 
Image source, Bruno Boelpaep/BBC Image caption, 
Upcoming presidential elections offer a crossroad, with polls predicting a run-off between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon 
We repeatedly approached French intelligence. They didn't want to comment. A sign perhaps of the huge sensitivity of the current situation, especially with France hurtling towards an extremely charged presidential election. 
But Michel Klein, a recently retired former police commissioner, told me he didn't think the radical left posed a serious threat to the French state. 
"I believe there is a will from the radical left and the anarchists to try and destroy the Republic but they obviously don't have the means to do it," he told me. 
He sees no risk of civil war in France (a possibility you hear some in the country discuss these days) but he identified a rising risk of clashes between far-left and far-right groups ahead of the presidential election. 
Polls currently predict a run-off in the vote between nationalist candidate Marine Le Pen and anticapitalist Mélenchon. 
Far-right vigilante groups have begun appearing on the edge of protests in a number of cities across France to "protect French streets", they say. 
The popular hard-left presidential candidate Mélenchon attends most demos, his supporters handing political pamphlets to the chanting crowds, but he denies any links with violence. 
France is so polarised, there's little sign next year's presidential vote will calm things. This turbulent mix of left and right, social and political unrest, feels like a perfect storm.

articles.title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
articles.summary: Days after resigning while mired in scandal of extra-marital affairs, Nvidia's Jensen Huang is making a remarkable return.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP By Michael Race ,  Peter Hoskins   and   Lucy Hooker ,  Business reporters 
- Published 12 November 2026 Updated 23 November 2026 
It's being called a comeback for the ages. 
For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong. 
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned. 
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company. 
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China? 
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg. 
But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology. 
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses. 
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping. 
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn. 
Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream. 
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. 
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia. 
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia. 
The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology. 
- 
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation 
- 
Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive? 
- Published 12 November 
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products. 
So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships. 
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. 
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit". 
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said. 
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him". 
First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset. 
Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family. 
But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down. 
He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was launched, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters. 
The man himself said he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him. 
Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.summary: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.
articles.full_text:
Image source, San Francisco Travel Association Image caption, 
The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector By Zoe Corbyn Technology reporter ,  Reporting from San Francisco 
- Published 23 November 2026 
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans. 
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups. 
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors. 
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver. 
Image source, Lauren Goldboss Image caption, 
Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers 
Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange. 
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up , external in San Francisco. 
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts. 
But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn , external that this was a possibility. 
Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn). 
-

- Published 5 days ago 
- 
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal 
- Published 13 hours ago 
- 
Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring 
- Published 9 July 
- 
Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now? 
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash? 
One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name. 
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China. 
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?" 
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible". 
Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity. 
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great." 
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south. 
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley. 
One study , external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley. 
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear. 
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn. 
"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank. 
Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth". 
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley. 
Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn. 
Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking. 
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says. 
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken. 
Image caption, 
Huge data centres are being built across the US to power AI 
But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing, , external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn. 
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco. 
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory. 
"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy." 
As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help. 
For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country 
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says 
A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said. 
Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad. 
Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage. Read more 
The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000). 
An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate. 
After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website. 
The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed. 
The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin. 
“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions. 
The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment. 
In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.

The US and Russia lack the power to impose their will on the continent – the Shenzhen summit was no Yalta 2.0 
T he first ever trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin was rich in symbolism and empty of substance. Many Europeans, filled with anxiety about the Chinese, Russian and US presidents potentially colluding, saw chilling echoes of the Yalta conference in 1945, when Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt redrew the map of Europe. 
But those – particularly in eastern Europe – who are fretting about another historic betrayal should remember that when it comes to European security today, we are the ones who hold most of the cards. Far more meaningful last week than Shenzhen was a gathering in Berlin , held at exactly the same time. 
True, the Shenzhen summit brought together three autocratic leaders who would like to see the world carved up into spheres of influence, but their meeting turned out to be no Yalta 2.0. The original Yalta took place as the second world war drew to a close, when international law and multilateral organisations were little more than a pipedream. The world was still living in an age of empire, with many colonies in the hands of European countries and the Soviet Union eager to consolidate its own in eastern Europe . It was hardly surprising, back then, that the war’s victors, the US, the UK and the USSR, held the keys to Europe’s future. 
Nothing of the kind was ever going to happen in Shenzhen, nor will it at any future gathering of Xi, Trump and Putin alone. Two of the three – Putin and Trump – cannot win the wars they have launched against Ukraine and Iran respectively. The third, Xi, by far the strongest of the trio, is doing little more than bask in the colossal mistakes of his American and Russian friends. EU proposes €45bn loan for Ukraine to avert cash crisis and boost defences 
Read more 
This is not to say that the three are irrelevant to Europe’s security. Russia and the US hold the world’s largest nuclear arsenals. Had Trump, Putin and Xi committed to nuclear arms control, as Trump wanted , Europe (and the rest of the world) would have applauded. But the Russian and Chinese leaders were never going to indulge Trump on that score. Possessing nuclear weapons is the only reason Putin can still claim a seat at the top table; without them, Russia would be little more than a second-rate power. China, meanwhile, in its scramble for superpower status, is racing to expand its nuclear arsenal, and catch up with the US and Russia. 
Russia, China and the US also matter in other dimensions of security. Putin’s Russia continues its military assault on Ukraine, which faces its hardest winter since Russia invaded. And Russia’s cyber-attacks, drone incursions, sabotage, attacks on critical infrastructure and disinformation campaigns across Europe have escalated to the point that it makes little sense to keep talking about “hybrid war”, or even “shadow war”. It would perhaps be more honest simply to call it what it is: Russia’s war against Europe. 
Russia is hardly fighting this war alone. China is not a direct participant, but has provided economic and technological support that has been vital to Russia’s war machine. Yet for all their efforts, there is no sign that Ukraine, or indeed any other European country, will fold – and this despite the fact that Trump’s US has all but switched sides. Washington no longer provides economic or military support to Ukraine. And while it still cooperates on intelligence and satellite communications, it has sickeningly tried to pressure Kyiv into capitulating by temporarily cutting off or slowing down these services. The US still has the capacity to inflict real damage on Ukraine and Europe. But Trump has failed to subjugate Ukraine over the last two years, and given his Republican party’s bruising defeat in the US midterm elections, he is unlikely to succeed in the next two. 
View image in fullscreen 
French armed forces minister Catherine Vautrin, Poland’s deputy prime minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, and UK defence secretary Wes Streeting during military exercises in Poland on 20 November 2026. Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/Shutterstock 
Trump, Putin and Xi may like a world in which, to borrow from Thucydides, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Their agreement in Shenzhen to oppose the alleged overreach of international tribunals – established to disprove that might makes right – signals exactly this. But the three men are not as strong as they would like to believe, nor is today’s world the Hobbesian wasteland over which Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin had the power to rule unchallenged. International law and multilateralism are under attack – but they are not dead. Middle powers in the global south are rising and making their voices heard. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion Trump could be about to sell out Ukraine. Europe must get its act together, fast | Paul Taylor 
Read more 
And Europe, though facing serious security threats, has far more leverage than is often recognised. Last week’s meeting in Berlin – where representatives of 36 countries in the French- and British-led coalition of the willing gathered to shore up support for Ukraine – was a show of strength far more concrete than the empty words in Shenzhen. 
The group agreed to close Ukraine’s funding gap for 2027: the EU has pledged an additional €45bn , with a further €25bn coming from non-EU coalition members such as the UK, Norway and Canada. And while the last time the EU agreed on a loan to Ukraine guaranteed by the EU budget, it allowed Hungary and Slovakia to opt out, today it is in no mood to tolerate dropouts. With negotiations on the next seven-year EU budget entering a critical phase, Germany, the largest net contributor, will oppose any budget deal unless all EU members agree to support Ukraine. 
Europe’s main problem is not material but political and, above all, psychological. Learned helplessness, towards the US in particular, is what fuels fears of the ghosts of Yalta, and a new betrayal. And it is because Europe still takes the Trump-Putin peace-talks charade too seriously that it spends so much time squabbling over who should represent it at that table. 
No peace plan pushed through by Putin and Trump will deliver Ukraine’s surrender, let alone a new security architecture for Europe. On their own, the two autocrats lack the power to impose their will. The more energy Europe devotes to delivering on the plans and pledges of the coalition of the willing, and the less it spends chasing the two failing leaders in Moscow and Washington, the more secure and peaceful tomorrow’s Europe will be.

But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.
